result: The study recruited 24 healthy right-handed participants (age 19-28, 17 females, 7 males) with sample size determined a priori based on prior similar studies. Two participants were excluded from eye-tracking analysis due to glasses, and one from EEG analysis due to artifacts. The study received ethical approval and participants provided informed consent.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C52-C54 provide complete methodological documentation of participant recruitment, exclusions, and ethical procedures. The sample size justification (C2) is reasonable based on prior work, though power analysis would strengthen this. Exclusion criteria are clearly stated and appropriate.

result: Behavioral performance showed no difference in reproduction accuracy across cue-reliability conditions, but reaction times were faster with more reliable cues. In 80% and 60% reliable-cue blocks, both accuracy and RT were better for validly vs. invalidly cued items, with larger cue-validity effects following 80% vs. 60% cues for RT but not accuracy.
evaluation: Claims C5-C13, C40, C90-C93 present consistent behavioral findings with appropriate statistical tests (ANOVAs, t-tests) and effect sizes. The graded behavioral effects as a function of cue reliability are well-documented. However, the non-significant accuracy difference between 80% and 60% conditions (C13) may reflect insufficient power rather than true equivalence.

result: Alpha lateralization (8-12 Hz) was observed in all four cue-reliability conditions with characteristic posterior topography. The magnitude of alpha lateralization was graded as a function of cue reliability, with stronger lateralization following more reliable cues, confirmed by significant main effect and linear trend.
evaluation: Claims C14-C18 demonstrate robust alpha lateralization effects with appropriate cluster-based permutation testing and ANOVA. The graded modulation by cue reliability replicates prior work (C16 cites Fu et al., 2022; Gould et al., 2011; Günseli et al., 2019; Haegens et al., 2012). Statistical evidence is strong with multiple converging analyses.

result: Spatial saccade bias toward the cued memory item was observed following cues in imperative-100%, 100%, and 80% conditions, but not significantly in the 60% condition. The bias was graded by cue reliability and predominantly driven by micro-saccades (<2° visual angle) rather than large saccades to encoded locations. This is the first demonstration of graded modulation of this gaze marker.
evaluation: Claims C19-C25, C94, C95, C119-C120 provide strong evidence for saccade bias with appropriate statistical testing. The micro-saccade characterization (C23, C94) is well-supported by saccade-size decomposition analysis. The novelty claim (C119) appears justified given prior work only used 100% reliable cues. The non-significant 60% condition (C22, p=0.341) may reflect reduced effect size or power limitations.

result: Following the memory test, alpha lateralization showed only weak spatial modulation, with only the 80% condition showing significant effects. In contrast, saccade bias showed clear patterns: opposite-direction bias in 100% conditions (likely reflecting return saccades), and toward-direction bias in 80% and 60% conditions for both valid and invalid trials.
evaluation: Claims C26-C30, C80-C81 reveal differential sensitivity of the two markers to test-locked re-orienting. The interpretation that large central test stimuli may attenuate alpha (C81) is plausible but speculative. The robust saccade effects in 80%/60% conditions but not 100% conditions represent a key finding distinguishing certain vs. uncertain test expectations.

result: Unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests did not delay the onset of saccade bias re-orienting but significantly prolonged its offset latency compared to expected tests, in both 80% and 60% conditions. This was confirmed by both jackknife and fractional area latency analyses, and remained robust when matching trial numbers between conditions.
evaluation: Claims C31-C39, C51, C77-C78, C104-C105 provide converging evidence from multiple latency analysis methods and robustness checks. The dissociation between onset (no difference) and offset (prolonged for invalid) is well-documented with Bayesian factors supporting null effects for onset. This represents a novel finding about the temporal dynamics of internal re-orienting.

result: Attentional deployment after the memory test only occurred when cues left uncertainty about which item would be tested (80%/60% conditions), not when cues were 100% reliable. Critically, this re-orienting occurred following both expected and unexpected tests, suggesting a second-stage verification ('double checking') process even when the tested item was already attended after the cue.
evaluation: Claims C72-C76, C82, C86, C100 present a key conceptual finding. The absence of test-locked re-orienting in 100% conditions is well-supported by data. The 'double checking' interpretation (C76, C82) is reasonable but somewhat speculative. The mechanistic explanations for why 100% cues eliminate test-locked re-orienting (C73-C75) cite relevant prior work but remain inferential.

result: Trial-sorting analysis based on whether participants showed toward-saccades after the cue revealed that test-locked attentional deployment occurred regardless of prior cue use. The magnitude of test-locked bias was not contingent on having previously oriented after the cue, with Bayesian factors supporting the null hypothesis across conditions.
evaluation: Claims C106-C111 provide critical evidence that test-locked re-orienting is not simply driven by trials where participants ignored the cue. The trial-sorting approach is methodologically sound, though the classification of 'cue use' based on single-trial saccades has limitations acknowledged by the authors. The Bayesian analyses (C109) strengthen the null findings. The interpretation of verification vs. genuine re-orienting (C111) is reasonable but speculative.

result: The prolonged attentional deployment following unexpected tests likely reflects prolonged effort to extract information from the unexpectedly tested memory item. The saccade bias in 100% conditions likely reflects return saccades to center from lingering cue-induced biases.
evaluation: Claims C79, C83, C98, C99, C108 provide mechanistic interpretations of the observed effects. While these interpretations are plausible and consistent with the data, they remain speculative without direct evidence linking prolonged re-orienting to information extraction processes. Alternative explanations (e.g., suppressing learned tendencies) are mentioned but not fully tested.

result: The experimental design manipulated cue reliability (100% imperative, 100%, 80%, 60%) with memory items presented laterally (6° eccentricity) and test items centrally. EEG (64-channel, 1024 Hz) and eye-tracking (1000 Hz) were recorded simultaneously. Data preprocessing included ICA artifact removal, time-frequency decomposition, and velocity-based saccade detection. Statistical analyses used cluster-based permutation testing with 10,000 permutations.
evaluation: Claims C48, C55-C71 provide comprehensive methodological documentation. The experimental design is well-suited to address the research questions. Data acquisition and preprocessing procedures are standard and appropriate. The saccade detection algorithm (C65-C67) is clearly described. Statistical methods (C70-C71) are appropriate for time-series data. Trial counts after preprocessing (C61) are adequate.

result: Prior work has established that attention can be directed to internal working memory representations and that the brain uses memorized locations for spatial orienting. Studies on external attention have characterized both orienting and re-orienting, but internal attention research has focused almost exclusively on orienting following retrocues. The current study uniquely addresses re-orienting in response to memory tests by presenting tests centrally while memory items were lateralized.
evaluation: Claims C41-C47, C87-C88, C112-C116 accurately characterize prior literature and identify a genuine gap. The citations are appropriate and comprehensive. The distinction between anticipatory re-orienting (prior work) and test-driven re-orienting (current work) is clearly articulated (C113). The methodological advantage of central test presentation (C116) is valid.

result: The study brings attentional re-orienting to the domain of working memory by demonstrating that internal attentional deployment following expected tests is not contingent on prior orienting (suggesting verification), while re-focusing following unexpected tests is prolonged. The central presentation of memory tests enabled isolation of spatial re-orienting in mind.
evaluation: Claims C49-C50, C84, C89 summarize the main conceptual contributions. These are well-supported by the empirical findings. The novelty of bringing re-orienting concepts from external to internal attention (C84) is justified. The experimental design rationale (C89) is sound.

result: Several methodological limitations and interpretive challenges are acknowledged: direct comparison between alpha and saccade markers is non-trivial; the link between gaze bias and RT was only established in one condition possibly due to insufficient trial numbers; whether graded effects reflect graded single-trial allocation or all-or-none allocation in a proportion of trials cannot be determined.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97, C102-C103, C117-C118 appropriately acknowledge limitations. The recognition that graded trial-average effects may not reflect graded single-trial allocation (C117-C118) is an important caveat. The limited behavioral correlations (C102-C103) may indeed reflect power issues. These honest assessments strengthen the overall evaluation.

result: Both cue-locked and test-locked attentional effects were predominantly reflected in fixational micro-saccades (<2° visual angle) rather than large saccades back to the original encoded locations (6° eccentricity).
evaluation: Claims C101, C23, C94 are well-supported by saccade-size decomposition analyses shown in figures. This finding is consistent with prior work from the same lab and strengthens the interpretation that these effects reflect internal attentional processes rather than overt spatial orienting to remembered locations.
